To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
China is a risk-averse actor that is pursuing a counterweight strategy to avoid overdependence on the G-7-centered financial order while maintaining collaborative relations.
China has pursued a risk-averse ‘counterweight strategy’, that is, developing a regional alternative while maintaining collaborative relations at the global level.

China has been pursuing an approach to regional and global financial governance that is risk-averse and that it seeks to avoid both overdependence on G7-centred global financial institutions while maintaining collaborative ties to them and overdependence on regional financial institutions while maintaining ties to them.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following question: What are the implications of China's multilateral behavior on the global financial governance structure?
the following questions: (a) how do the Chinese perceive the role and function of the IMF and the World Bank?
the question of whether China is likely to be assimilated into the existing global financial order or whether it is likely to be a disruptive force in that order.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
China is not a threat to the existing international financial system, but it is a challenge.
China's multilateral strategy is not about the choice between confrontation and assimilation, but about a more fragmented and more complex global financial order.
China is not assimilating into the liberal world order but is also not seeking to destroy that order.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
China has been pursuing both global and regional financial institutions in order to maintain a wide range of strategic options.
the article argues for the need to understand China's multilateral behavior as part of the process of fragmentation in global governance.
China is neither a passive follower nor an active challenger of the US-led liberal order.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the global financial crisis has not only changed the global financial order, but also the way in which the United States and China interact.
the United States and other G-7 countries should not expect China to accept the current global order and its institutions without any change.
, as a rising power, China is not a passive follower in international institutions but an active shaper of the rules of the game.
